verses.text: After the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, took leave of them, and departed to go into Macedonia.
When he had gone through those parts, and had encouraged them with many words, he came into Greece.
When he had spent three months there, and a plot was made against him by Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he determined to return through Macedonia.
These accompanied him as far as Asia: Sopater of Beroea; Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians; Gaius of Derbe; Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia.
But these had gone ahead, and were waiting for us at Troas.
We sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and continued his speech until midnight.
There were many lights in the upper room where we  were gathered together.

A certain young man named Eutychus sat in the window, weighed down with deep sleep. As Paul spoke still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he fell down from the third floor, and was taken up dead.
Paul went down, and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”
When he had gone up, and had broken bread, and eaten, and had talked with them a long while, even until break of day, he departed.
They brought the boy in alive, and were greatly comforted.
But we, going ahead to the ship, set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for he had so arranged, intending himself to go by land.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard, and came to Mitylene.
Sailing from there, we came the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we came to Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus, that he might not have to spend time in Asia; for he was hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus, and called to himself the elders of the assembly.
When they had come to him, he said to them, “You yourselves know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time,
serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews;
how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house,
testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus.
Now, behold, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there;
except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me.

But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.
“Now, behold, I know that you all, among whom I went about preaching God’s Kingdom, will see my face no more.
Therefore I testify to you today that I am clean from the blood of all men,
for I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.
Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and  God which he purchased with his own blood.
For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them.
Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.
Now, brothers,  I entrust you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up, and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
I coveted no one’s silver, or gold, or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me.
In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
When he had spoken these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all.
They all wept a lot, and fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him,
sorrowing most of all because of the word which he had spoken, that they should see his face no more. And they accompanied him to the ship.

footnotes.content: Even after the city has calmed, Paul doesn't rush away—he gathers his disciples to say goodbye. That's the mark of a shepherd: in the chaos, you think of the flock first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He moves through the region speaking words of encouragement—not grand speeches, just presence and truth. The Lord often works through a faithful word whispered into a tired heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three months in Greece, then a plot against him. Paul could have sailed away—instead he changes course, trusting the Spirit's leading even when danger shows itself. That's faith without bravado.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These companions—from Beroea, Thessalonica, Derbe, and Asia—each represent a church that caught fire with the Gospel. Paul doesn't travel alone; the Body moves with him, carrying gifts and prayers from every corner.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul sends the brothers ahead while he lingers. Patient love often means letting others go first, trusting the timing is held in a wiser hand than our own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philippi to Troas takes five days by ship—a familiar journey, yet every crossing is a small trust. They left after Passover week, and now gather for a Lord's Day meal: resurrection life moves through their calendar.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: First day of the week, gathered to break bread: the early church marks its life by the Resurrection. Paul talks until midnight—not to show off, but because the hour is short and the love is too full to contain in ordinary words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many lamps burning through the darkness—a small sign of the light they carry, gathered in that upper room. Even ordinary detail speaks to how the Body treasures these last hours together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eutychus nods off, then tumbles from the third floor. In one breath, death seems certain. But notice—even the tragedy becomes a stage for the Lord's mercy. He doesn't let the night steal what belongs to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul runs down, embraces the boy, and speaks the words he believes: 'His life is in him.' That's not magic—it's a shepherd's certainty born of knowing whose hand holds all breath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After raising the boy, Paul breaks bread and talks until dawn. Some might hurry away from such a night, but he stays, feeds his flock, and speaks. Love doesn't leave; it lingers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring Eutychus in alive—and the comfort that floods those believers is more than relief. It's the felt nearness of a God who cares for every tender thing. That morning, they understood grace a little deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul arranges to walk overland while the others sail ahead. He's deliberate about his movements, never wasting a moment—yet never rushing so hard he forgets to pray, to walk, to be present to the land beneath his feet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Assos is a port town on the Aegean coast—Paul walks there and joins the ship. Even these small routings matter: the faithful life is made of thousands of small obediences, each one a love-letter to the One who directs our steps.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chios, Samos, Trogyllium, Miletus—each harbor a waypoint. The coastline unfolds like a story, and Paul knows it now. These places have become holy ground because the Gospel has walked there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul sails *past* Ephesus—the very city where he spent years—so he might reach Jerusalem for Pentecost. Some missions require us to say no even to beloved places, trusting that the One who calls us knows the whole map.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Miletus he sends for the elders of Ephesus to come. Rather than enter the city himself, he brings them to him. There's something sacred here—a final gathering, like a father summoning his household.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul reminds them: 'You know how I was with you from the first day I set foot in Asia.' He's not distant or theoretical—he stands in memory with them, present in all that was built together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Serving with humility, tears, trials—he names the cost. A true shepherd doesn't hide the cost of love; he shows it openly so others learn that sacrifice is the language the Kingdom speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Teaching publicly and house to house—the Gospel moves through both the town square and the kitchen table. No one is beneath the message; no gathering too small for truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Repentance toward God and faith toward Jesus—he testifies to both Jews and Greeks the same turning point. The Gospel doesn't change its name; it calls all people to turn and believe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul knows the Spirit is binding him to Jerusalem, but he doesn't know what waits there. That's the peculiar courage of faithfulness: you follow into uncertainty, held by the hand of One who sees the whole story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bonds and afflictions wait for him—the Holy Spirit testifies ahead of time. Paul faces what's coming with eyes open, neither courting suffering nor fleeing it, but walking steady into the will of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in these words: 'These things don't count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself.' Paul has already counted the cost and found it light compared to finishing his race with joy. That same Spirit still calls believers to lay down lesser loves for the greatest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tells them plainly: 'You will see my face no more.' This is not a temporary goodbye—it's a final parting. He speaks it with sorrow, yes, but also with the peace of one who knows his work is complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul testifies he is clean from the blood of all men—he held back nothing of what they needed to hear. That's the shepherd's final plea: I gave you everything the Lord gave me.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He didn't shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God. Not the comfortable parts, not the popular parts—the whole counsel. That's the mark of one who loves truth more than approval.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul calls them to be overseers—shepherds—of the flock purchased with Christ's own blood. That's no small thing. Every soul they guard has been ransomed at infinite cost; they hold the treasure of heaven in their hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After he's gone, wolves will come—not gentle, not sparing the flock. Paul doesn't hide the danger; he names it so the shepherds stay watchful. Love and vigilance go together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: False teachers will rise from among their own—even from those they know. The deepest wounds come from familiar hands. Paul warns them so their eyes stay open and their hearts stay guarded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For three years he didn't cease to admonish, night and day, with tears. That's the cost of loving a flock: staying awake, staying tender, staying faithful when no one's looking. He earned the right to speak this warning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Paul entrusts them to God and to the word of His grace. He lets go of what he's poured into them, trusting that grace is greater than his hands can hold. That's how a true leader leads: by learning to release.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul reminds them he coveted no one's silver, gold, or clothing. He served them freely, held their affection lightly. A leader's integrity is measured by what he doesn't grasp.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These hands worked to meet his own needs and those with him. Paul labored with his own hands, not demanding of the flock. That's the humility that earns a hearing: you show your people you don't ask them to carry what you won't carry yourself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He quotes the Lord Jesus: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.' This saying isn't elsewhere recorded in the Gospels—Paul carries it as a treasure from the risen Christ. He gives them a word they'll turn over in their hearts for years.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After all his words, Paul kneels down to pray. He doesn't end with speeches—he ends on his knees. That's where a pastor's final authority comes from: not eloquence, but intercession.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They all weep and fall on his neck and kiss him. No one stands apart; the entire room breaks open in love. That's what it looks like when a flock has truly been shepherded—they cling to the one who gave them himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They grieve most because they'll see his face no more. He walks to the ship, and they watch him go. Sometimes love means learning how to say goodbye, holding the memory of faithfulness even when the faithful one departs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
